providedBy.short: A contract with the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office
providedBy.text: Lafayette's police are a contract with the Contra Costa County Sheriff: $6,454,458 of this program pays the Sheriff, and the City's latest financial report counts 16 contracted sworn officers. The program also pays for County animal control ($336,923). Much of the contract's 30.8% rise is a move, not new spending: this budget folds Traffic Enforcement and the Supplementary Law Enforcement fund into Police Services.

cites.quote: This program provides contract law enforcement services to the community via the Contra Costa Sheriff's Department.

questions.question: Is this everything the City of Lafayette spends?

paragraphs.text: No. These pages show the City's [General Fund](glossary:General Fund), its main account for day-to-day services: {generalFund} in {year}. The City also keeps separate funds, for capital projects, recreation programs, the library, school buses and more, and those aren't in the squares on these pages.

paragraphs.text: Public schools in Lafayette are run by separate governments. The Lafayette School District runs four elementary schools and a middle school, and the high school is in the Acalanes district, which also serves Canyon, Moraga, Orinda and parts of Walnut Creek.

cites.quote: The Lafayette School District operates 4 elementary schools and one middle school within the city boundary. The high school is in the Acalanes Unified High School District, which also serves the communities of Canyon, Moraga, Orinda, and portions of Walnut Creek.

paragraphs.text: The City isn't financially responsible for them, so school spending isn't in the City's numbers.

cites.quote: As a result, the City has only one component unit and no other legal entities for which it is financially or legally responsible.

questions.question: Where does my property tax go?

paragraphs.text: The basic 1% property tax is pooled by the county and divided under state law among the county, cities, schools and [special districts](glossary:Special District).

cites.quote: Your county auditor pools your 1 percent rate tax payment, as well as payments from other property owners in your county, into a single countywide pot.
State law directs how your county auditor distributes the revenue in the countywide pot.
your county auditor sets aside this $1,000 for your city, county, schools, and special districts.

paragraphs.text: The City says it receives about 6.6% of the property taxes its residents pay, against an average of 10.5% for other cities in Contra Costa County. It didn't levy a property tax before Proposition 13 passed in 1978, so the state's formula gives it a low share.

cites.quote: Currently, the City receives approximately 6.6% of the property taxes paid by its residents, compared to an average of 10.5% for other cities in Contra Costa.
the City did not levy a property tax prior to 1978 when Proposition 13 was adopted. Consequently, it receives a relatively low share of the property tax under the statutory formula.

paragraphs.text: The {propertyTax} in property tax on these pages is only the City's share.

questions.question: Does the City pay for the schools?

paragraphs.text: The City runs a school bus program from its own fund, outside the General Fund, and it took over the crossing guard program after the school district stopped funding it.

cites.quote: Following the School District's decision to discontinue its funding and management of the Crossing Guard program, the City assumed full program responsibility.

paragraphs.text: We haven't checked every line of the City's full budget, so small City grants or contracts with the districts can't be ruled out.
